questions.title: Merge vs. rebase, conceptually
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between git merge and git rebase when bringing a feature branch up to date with main, and what's the real tradeoff between them?
questions.modelAnswer: git merge takes the two branches' histories and creates a new merge commit that ties them together, preserving the exact history of both branches as they actually happened, including a visible merge point. git rebase instead takes your branch's commits and replays them one by one on top of the current tip of main, producing a linear history that looks as if you had branched off the latest main all along -- but it rewrites commit hashes in the process, which is the real tradeoff: rebase gives a cleaner, linear history that's easier to read later, but rewriting history on a branch that others have already pulled and based work on causes real problems for them, since their local history no longer matches. The practical rule is rebase is safe on a local or not-yet-shared branch to clean up history before opening a pull request, and merge (or at minimum, extreme caution) is the right call once a branch is shared with others.
questions.professionalAnswer: Merge preserves exactly what happened -- both branches' real commit history, tied together with a merge commit -- so you can always see that a merge happened and when. Rebase rewrites your branch's commits so they look like they were made on top of main's current tip, which gives you a clean, linear history, but it does that by actually creating new commits with new hashes, discarding the old ones. That's the real tradeoff: rebase's history is nicer to read, but rewriting history is dangerous the moment someone else has already pulled your branch and built on top of the old commits, because now their history and yours have diverged in a confusing way. My rule of thumb is simple -- rebase freely on my own branch before I've shared it with anyone, to clean things up before opening a PR, but once it's pushed and someone else might be working off it, I switch to merge, or I at least ask before rebasing something shared.

Safe rule: rebase on unshared/local branches, merge (or caution) once a branch is shared

questions.title: What systemd Actually Controls for a Service
questions.prompt: You run `systemctl enable --now myapp`. What does `enable` actually do versus `start`, and what's actually inside the unit file that makes a service restart automatically if it crashes?
questions.modelAnswer: `enable` and `start` are independent actions: `enable` creates a symlink into the appropriate systemd target's wants directory so the service is launched automatically on every future boot, while `start` actually launches the process right now, in the current session, with no effect on boot behavior. Running them together is common specifically because you usually want both: start it now and keep it starting on every boot. Automatic restart on crash isn't something the application has to implement -- it's controlled by the `Restart=` directive in the unit file's `[Service]` section (for example `Restart=on-failure`), paired with `RestartSec=` for the delay between attempts; systemd itself is responsible for watching the process and relaunching it according to that policy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of `enable` and `start` as answering two separate questions: enable answers 'should this launch automatically on boot,' start answers 'is it running right now.' You can enable a service without starting it (it'll come up next reboot but isn't running yet), or start one without enabling it (running now, but won't survive a reboot), which is why `--now` exists as a shortcut for doing both at once. On the restart behavior, that's not application code at all -- it's a line in the unit file's `[Service]` block, `Restart=on-failure` or `Restart=always`, plus `RestartSec=` for how long to wait before trying again. systemd is the thing watching the process and relaunching it per that policy, which is also why editing a unit file requires `systemctl daemon-reload` before the new behavior actually takes effect.
commonMistakes: Assuming start also enables the service on boot, or vice versa
Forgetting that automatic restart is a unit file directive, not something the app must implement
Not distinguishing Restart=on-failure from Restart=always
Editing a unit file without running systemctl daemon-reload afterward
keyPoints: enable creates a boot-time symlink; start launches the process immediately; they're independent
Restart= and RestartSec= in [Service] control automatic restart behavior
systemd, not the application, is responsible for relaunching a crashed process
daemon-reload is required after editing a unit file for changes to take effect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes enable vs start
Correctly explains Restart= directive and systemd's role
Mentions daemon-reload requirement

questions.title: Why SSH Key Pairs Are Safer Than Passwords, Mechanically
questions.prompt: Explain, mechanically, how SSH public-key authentication actually proves your identity to a server without ever sending your private key over the network, and why that's fundamentally different from password authentication.
questions.modelAnswer: The server holds your public key in `authorized_keys`. During authentication, the server issues a cryptographic challenge, and your client proves possession of the matching private key by signing it -- the private key itself never has to be transmitted anywhere, because asymmetric cryptography lets the server verify that signature using only the public key it already has. Password authentication works completely differently: the secret itself (the password) has to be sent to the server, even over an encrypted channel, so the server can compare it, which means the secret genuinely leaves your machine on every login. With key-based auth, the one thing that actually matters is never transmitted at all, which is why a network capture or a compromised server can't hand an attacker your private key the way it potentially could with a password.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I explain it: with a password, the actual secret has to travel to the server every time you log in, even if it's encrypted in transit -- the server needs to see it to check it. With a key pair, the server never needs to see your private key at all. It sends a challenge, your client signs it with the private key, and the server checks that signature against the public key it already has on file -- the math proves you hold the private key without it ever leaving your machine. That's a fundamentally smaller exposure surface: a server breach or a network capture can't hand someone your private key the way it could expose a password. The one thing I'd add is that the private key file itself should have its own passphrase, so even if someone steals the file off disk, they still need that passphrase to actually use it -- the key pair mechanism is only as safe as how well you protect the private key locally.

Treating a passphrase-less private key file as equally safe as one with a passphrase
Not understanding what authorized_keys actually stores (public key, not shared secret)
Confusing key-based auth with just 'typing less'

The private key never leaves the client machine

questions.title: SIGTERM vs. SIGKILL, and Why the Difference Matters
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between sending a process SIGTERM and SIGKILL, and why does that difference matter for a service doing something like writing to a database when it's told to stop?
questions.modelAnswer: SIGTERM is a polite request that a process can intercept and handle, giving it a chance to clean up -- close file handles, finish writing a buffer, close database connections -- before actually exiting. SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored at all; the kernel terminates the process immediately, with zero opportunity for any cleanup code to run. That difference matters directly for something like a database write in progress: an abrupt SIGKILL mid-write can leave data corrupted or a transaction half-committed, while a process that handles SIGTERM can finish the current write, close its connection cleanly, and then exit, avoiding that risk entirely. This is also exactly why systemd's default stop sequence sends SIGTERM first and only escalates to SIGKILL after a timeout if the process hasn't exited on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: SIGTERM is the signal I think of as 'please wrap up and exit' -- a well-written service can catch it, finish whatever it's in the middle of, close its connections cleanly, and then actually exit. SIGKILL is different in kind, not just severity: the process can't catch it, can't ignore it, can't run any cleanup code at all, the kernel just ends it immediately. For something stateful, like a service mid-write to a database, that difference is the whole point -- getting SIGKILL mid-transaction can leave things half-done or corrupted, where a graceful SIGTERM handler would have finished or safely rolled back first. That's also exactly why systemd's own stop behavior sends SIGTERM, waits a configurable amount of time, and only reaches for SIGKILL if the process is still stubbornly running -- SIGKILL is the last resort, not the default.
commonMistakes: Assuming SIGKILL can be caught/handled like SIGTERM
Using kill -9 as the default instead of a plain kill (SIGTERM) first
Not giving a process time to shut down gracefully before escalating to SIGKILL
Forgetting systemd's default stop sequence already sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after a timeout
keyPoints: SIGTERM can be caught/handled; SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored
Graceful shutdown handling lets an app finish in-flight work before exiting
Abrupt termination risks data corruption for stateful work like database writes
systemd's stop sequence sends SIGTERM, waits, then SIGKILL if still running

questions.title: Why Environment Variables Beat Hardcoded Secrets in a Script
questions.prompt: Why is reading a secret from an environment variable in a Python or Bash automation script meaningfully safer than hardcoding it directly in the script file, and what's a gap that environment variables alone don't close?
questions.modelAnswer: A hardcoded secret gets committed to source control along with the rest of the script, visible to anyone with repository access and permanently present in git history even after it's later removed from the current file. Reading it from an environment variable keeps the actual value out of the codebase entirely -- it's supplied at runtime by the shell, the CI system, or a secrets manager, so the code that gets reviewed and shared never contains the real value at all. The gap environment variables don't close is that the value is still plaintext once the process is running: anyone with sufficient privilege can read it from `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and it can easily leak if a script accidentally logs or prints its own environment during debugging. Env vars are a real improvement over hardcoding, but they aren't full secrets management -- they don't give you rotation, access auditing, or protection from an accidental log leak the way a dedicated secrets manager does.
questions.professionalAnswer: Hardcoding a secret means it's sitting in the file, which means it's sitting in git -- and even if you delete it in a later commit, it's still fully recoverable from history, which a lot of people don't realize until it's a real incident. Reading it from an environment variable means the actual value never has to be in the code at all -- whoever's reviewing my script sees `os.environ['API_KEY']`, not the key itself. But I don't treat that as 'solved' -- the value is still plaintext in the running process's environment, so anyone with enough access to the machine can read it off `/proc`, and the easiest way I've seen it leak in practice is someone debugging a script and accidentally printing the whole environment or logging a request that includes it. So env vars are genuinely better than hardcoding, but they're not a substitute for an actual secrets manager if you need real rotation and auditing.

Printing or logging an env var's value during debugging, leaking it into logs
Committing a .env file with real secrets to source control
Not rotating a secret after it's been exposed via logs or /proc

Real secrets management adds rotation, auditing, and access control env vars alone don't provide

questions.title: Why Kubernetes and CI Pipelines Default to YAML, Not JSON
questions.prompt: JSON and YAML can both represent the same configuration data. Why do tools like Kubernetes and most CI/CD systems default to YAML for config files instead of JSON, and what real problems does YAML's own syntax introduce in exchange?
questions.modelAnswer: YAML supports comments, is visually much less noisy than JSON (no braces or quotes scattered everywhere), and supports features like multi-document files and anchors, which makes large, hand-authored configuration meaningfully easier for a human to write and maintain -- JSON was designed primarily as a data-interchange format, not something meant to be hand-edited as config, and it has none of that. The tradeoff is real: YAML's structure is defined by indentation, so a single misplaced space can silently change the meaning of a file or break parsing in a way that's hard to spot visually, and YAML has well-documented surprises, like an unquoted `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off` getting silently interpreted as a boolean, or a version string like `1.10` being parsed as a number. JSON's explicit braces are more verbose, but they're structurally unambiguous in a way YAML's whitespace-driven syntax isn't.
questions.professionalAnswer: YAML wins for hand-written config mostly because it lets you write comments and doesn't bury the actual content in braces and quotes the way JSON does -- for a 200-line Kubernetes manifest or pipeline file, that readability difference is real. What it costs you is that the structure is defined by indentation, and a single misplaced space can quietly change what a block belongs to without throwing an obvious error, which is a genuinely common source of 'this worked yesterday' bugs. YAML also has some specific gotchas worth knowing by name -- an unquoted `yes` or `on` getting silently turned into a boolean, or a value like `1.10` getting parsed as a number and losing the trailing zero -- that have bitten people in pipeline configs. JSON doesn't have any of that ambiguity, but it also doesn't support comments at all, which is a real loss for anything meant to be maintained by humans over time.

Not knowing YAML silently coerces unquoted values like yes/no/on/off into booleans
Treating whitespace errors in YAML as a minor style issue rather than a parsing risk
Forgetting JSON doesn't support comments at all
keyPoints: YAML supports comments and a less verbose syntax, better suited to hand-authored config
JSON is explicit and unambiguous but was designed as a data-interchange format, not for humans to hand-write

The choice is a readability/maintainability tradeoff against strict unambiguous structure

questions.title: An Image Is Not a Container: What Actually Changes at Runtime
questions.prompt: What's the actual, technical difference between a Docker image and a container, and what specifically happens the moment you run `docker run` that turns one into the other?
questions.modelAnswer: An image is a read-only, layered filesystem snapshot plus metadata (default command, exposed ports, environment) -- it's inert, stored on disk, and never changes once built. `docker run` takes that image and creates a container: a running instance with its own thin writable layer stacked on top of the image's read-only layers, plus its own isolated process namespace, network namespace, and allocated resources. Any file changes a running container makes go into that writable layer, not the underlying image, which is exactly why you can run the same image many times as many independent containers, each with its own writable layer, without any of them affecting one another or the shared image underneath.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the image as the class and the container as the instance. The image is a frozen, read-only stack of filesystem layers sitting on disk -- it doesn't do anything by itself. The moment I run `docker run`, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of those read-only layers specifically for that one container, plus its own process and network namespaces, and that writable layer is where any file changes the running container makes actually land. That's the mechanism behind something people find surprising at first: I can run the same image ten times and get ten independent containers, each able to write its own files without touching the image or any of the other nine, and when a container is removed, that writable layer -- and whatever it wrote -- is gone unless it was explicitly persisted with a volume.

Assuming changes made inside a running container modify the underlying image
Not realizing multiple containers can run from the same image independently
Forgetting the writable layer is discarded when a container is removed, unless explicitly committed or using a volume

Multiple containers can run from one image independently, each with its own writable layer

questions.title: What Docker Compose Actually Solves
questions.prompt: You could run three separate containers with three separate `docker run` commands, each with its own flags for networking, ports, and environment variables. What does Docker Compose actually add on top of that, beyond just saving typing?
questions.modelAnswer: Compose's real value is declaring the whole multi-container application's desired state in one versioned YAML file -- services, their images or build context, networking, volumes, environment, and startup dependency order (`depends_on`) -- so the entire stack can be brought up or torn down as a single unit with one command, reproducibly, by anyone who has the file, not just whoever remembers the right flags. It also automatically creates a shared network connecting all defined services by service name, so containers can reach each other by name without any manual per-container network wiring that separate `docker run` commands would otherwise require. It's explicitly not a production orchestrator -- no multi-host scheduling, no self-healing -- it's a single-host tool for defining and running a multi-container application's lifecycle.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real win isn't fewer keystrokes, it's that the whole application's shape -- every service, how they're networked, what volumes they use, what order they should start in -- lives in one file that's checked into the repo, so anyone on the team gets the exact same stack by running one command instead of reconstructing a pile of flags from memory or a wiki page. It also quietly solves networking for you: every service defined in the file can reach every other service by its service name on a shared network Compose creates automatically, which is exactly the kind of thing that's tedious and error-prone to wire up by hand across separate `docker run` commands. What it isn't is a production orchestrator -- there's no multi-host scheduling or self-healing here, it's specifically a single-host tool for defining and running a multi-container app's lifecycle, mostly aimed at local development and simple deployments.

Treating Compose as a production-grade orchestrator with self-healing/scaling
Forgetting Compose's real value is reproducibility -- anyone with the file can stand up the identical stack

questions.title: Volumes vs. Bind Mounts: What Actually Differs
questions.prompt: Docker gives you both named volumes and bind mounts for persisting data outside a container. What's the actual difference in how each is managed, and when would picking the wrong one bite you?
questions.modelAnswer: A bind mount maps a specific path on the host filesystem directly into the container -- Docker doesn't manage or track that path's lifecycle at all, it's just whatever's really there, which makes it great for live-mounting source code during development but fragile across environments since it depends on that exact host directory structure existing. A named volume is fully managed by Docker, living in Docker's own storage area independent of any specific host path -- Docker handles its lifecycle (create, back up, remove), and it's portable across hosts since nothing depends on a particular host directory existing. Picking a bind mount for production persistent data ties that data to one host's specific filesystem path, breaking if the container moves to a different host; picking a named volume when you actually need live-editing of local source files means editing a file in your IDE won't be reflected the way a direct bind mount would.
questions.professionalAnswer: A bind mount is just pointing at a real folder on my machine and handing it to the container -- Docker doesn't know or care about that path beyond mounting it, which is exactly what I want when I'm live-editing source code locally and want the container to see my changes instantly. A named volume is different -- Docker owns it completely, it lives in Docker's own storage, and it's not tied to any specific folder on my machine, which is exactly what I want for something like a database's data directory that needs to survive the container being recreated and ideally move cleanly if this ever runs on a different host. The mistake I've seen bite people is using a bind mount for production data -- which quietly ties that data to one specific host's filesystem path and breaks the moment the container is scheduled somewhere else -- or reaching for a named volume when they actually just wanted to edit code locally and see it reflected immediately.

questions.title: Why Kubernetes' Smallest Unit Is a Pod, Not a Container
questions.prompt: Why does Kubernetes schedule and manage Pods rather than scheduling individual containers directly, and what does putting two containers in the same Pod actually guarantee that two separate Pods wouldn't?
questions.modelAnswer: A Pod is a thin wrapper around one or more containers meant to be deployed, scaled, and co-located together -- Kubernetes schedules the Pod as a single unit onto one node, and all containers inside that Pod share the same network namespace (same IP and port space, so they reach each other over localhost) and can share mounted volumes. Two containers in the same Pod are therefore guaranteed to always run on the same node, start and stop together, and communicate without any network hop -- exactly the contract a tightly coupled helper, like a logging sidecar reading files the main container writes, actually needs. Two separate Pods give no such guarantee: they can land on different nodes, scale independently, and share no localhost network, which is the right choice when components should genuinely be independent rather than tightly coupled.
questions.professionalAnswer: Kubernetes doesn't schedule individual containers at all -- the Pod is the actual unit it places onto a node, and that matters because of what it guarantees for anything inside it. Containers in the same Pod share a network namespace, so they talk to each other over localhost with no network hop, and they're guaranteed to be co-located on the same node and to start and stop together. That's exactly the right contract for something like a sidecar that needs to read log files the main container is writing -- they need to be on the same machine, reachable instantly, no exceptions. Two separate Pods don't give you any of that: they might land on different nodes entirely, they scale independently, and there's no shared localhost network between them, which is actually what you want when two components should genuinely be able to fail or scale independently rather than always moving together.

questions.title: How a Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod Actually Relate
questions.prompt: When you apply a Deployment manifest in Kubernetes, what object(s) does it actually create underneath it, and why does Kubernetes use that extra layer instead of just having the Deployment manage Pods directly?
questions.modelAnswer: Applying a Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, which is the object that actually owns and maintains a specified number of identical Pod replicas, and the ReplicaSet in turn creates the Pods themselves. The Deployment's real job sits one layer up: it manages ReplicaSets over time, which is specifically what enables rolling updates -- when you change the Deployment's Pod template (say, a new image tag), it creates a new ReplicaSet with the new template and gradually scales it up while scaling the old ReplicaSet down, keeping the old ReplicaSet around at zero replicas so a rollback can simply scale it back up instead of reconstructing the previous state from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer: A Deployment doesn't touch Pods directly -- it creates and owns a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet is the thing actually responsible for keeping the right number of Pods alive. The reason that extra layer exists is rolling updates: when I change the image tag in a Deployment, it doesn't edit the existing ReplicaSet in place, it creates a brand-new ReplicaSet with the new Pod template and shifts replicas from the old one to the new one gradually. The old ReplicaSet doesn't get deleted, it just gets scaled down to zero, which is exactly why a rollback is fast -- Kubernetes just scales the old ReplicaSet back up instead of having to rebuild the previous state from nothing. That's the whole reason for the extra object: it turns 'change the Pod template' into a safe, gradual, reversible operation instead of an all-at-once swap.

questions.title: ConfigMaps vs. Secrets: The Real Difference, Not Just the Name
questions.prompt: Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets are structurally almost identical -- both store key-value data and can be mounted the same ways. So what's the actual, practical reason to use a Secret instead of a ConfigMap for something like a database password?
questions.modelAnswer: Structurally they're nearly the same object, but Secrets get specific handling that ConfigMaps don't: Secret values are base64-encoded in the API by default -- which is just encoding, not encryption, an important distinction not to oversell -- Kubernetes can be explicitly configured to encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd, and kubectl/dashboard tooling masks Secret values in output by default in a way ConfigMap values aren't. Using a ConfigMap for a password means the plaintext value sits in plain view everywhere a ConfigMap might surface, including logs or tooling output that happens to dump it, and signals to every engineer reading the manifest that this value is safe to view and share, which a password definitely is not. The practical reason is intent and tooling behavior, not unbreakable encryption by default -- real production secret security still typically requires an external secrets manager or at-rest encryption configured explicitly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The structure is basically the same, so the real difference is in how the platform and its tooling treat the two types. Secret values are base64-encoded by default -- and I'm careful to say encoded, not encrypted, because that trips people up -- and kubectl and most dashboards specifically mask Secret contents in their output in a way they don't for ConfigMaps. If I put a database password in a ConfigMap, that plaintext value is going to show up in plain view anywhere a ConfigMap gets displayed, logged, or dumped, and it tells every other engineer reading the manifest 'this is fine to look at,' which a password isn't. The honest caveat is that a Secret alone doesn't give you real encryption at rest -- that requires explicitly configuring etcd encryption -- so for anything genuinely sensitive in production, I'd still want an actual secrets manager behind it, not just the Secret object by itself.

questions.title: Continuous Integration, Delivery, and Deployment Are Three Different Promises
questions.prompt: 'CI/CD' gets used as one phrase, but continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment are actually three different things. What does each one specifically guarantee, and where's the real line between delivery and deployment?
questions.modelAnswer: Continuous integration means developers merge code changes frequently into a shared branch, with an automated build and test run on every merge to catch integration problems early -- its guarantee stops at 'the code builds and passes tests,' not at releasing anything. Continuous delivery extends that by guaranteeing every change that passes the pipeline is automatically packaged into a deployable artifact and is release-ready at any time -- but an actual human still decides when to push the button to release it to production. Continuous deployment goes one step further and removes that human gate entirely: every change that passes the pipeline is automatically deployed to production with no manual approval step. The real line between delivery and deployment is specifically that manual release decision -- delivery keeps it, deployment automates it away.
questions.professionalAnswer: These three get flattened into one phrase constantly, but they're genuinely different promises. Continuous integration just promises that code merges frequently and gets built and tested automatically every time -- it says nothing at all about releasing. Continuous delivery promises more: every change that passes the pipeline is packaged and genuinely ready to release at any moment, but a person still has to decide to actually release it. Continuous deployment removes that person entirely -- anything that passes the pipeline goes straight to production, automatically, no approval step. If someone asks me where exactly delivery ends and deployment begins, my answer is always the same: it's that one manual release decision. Keep it, you're doing delivery. Automate it away, you're doing deployment.
commonMistakes: Treating CI, CD-delivery, and CD-deployment as synonyms for the same practice
Believing continuous delivery means code is automatically released to production without approval
Not identifying the manual release gate as the exact distinction between delivery and deployment
Assuming any pipeline with automated tests qualifies as continuous delivery
keyPoints: Continuous integration guarantees frequent merges with automated build/test, nothing about release
Continuous delivery guarantees a release-ready artifact exists at any time, pending a human decision to release
Continuous deployment removes that human gate and releases automatically on a passing pipeline
The actual dividing line between delivery and deployment is the manual approval/release step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines continuous integration
Correctly defines continuous delivery
Correctly defines continuous deployment
Correctly identifies the manual gate as the real distinction

questions.title: Resolving a merge conflict from the command line
questions.prompt: You run git merge and get a conflict in src/client.py. Walk through the actual git commands and steps you'd use to resolve it and complete the merge.
questions.modelAnswer: After the conflict is reported, open the conflicted file and look for git's conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), which bracket the competing versions from each branch; edit the file by hand to keep the correct combined content and remove all three marker lines completely -- leaving a marker in place is a common mistake that breaks the file. Then stage the resolved file with git add, confirm there are no remaining conflicts with git status, and complete the merge with git commit (git merge typically pre-fills a merge commit message, which can be kept or edited). If the merge turns out to be a mistake partway through, git merge --abort cleanly backs out before committing.
questions.professionalAnswer: First I open the file and look for the three conflict markers -- <<<<<<< HEAD marks the start of my current branch's version, ======= separates it from the incoming branch's version, and >>>>>>> marks the end of theirs. I read both sides, decide what the correct final content actually is (which might be one side, the other, or a combination), and edit the file directly to that final state, making sure I delete all three marker lines -- leaving one in is a mistake I've made before and it's an easy one to miss since the file still looks mostly fine. Once it looks right, git add the file to mark it resolved, run git status to confirm nothing else is still conflicted, and git commit to finish the merge. If partway through I realize this merge is more complicated than I want to untangle right now, git merge --abort gets me back to a clean state before I've committed anything.
questions.example:
# After git merge reports a conflict in src/client.py:
# 1. Open src/client.py, resolve the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> sections by hand
# 2. Stage the resolved file
git add src/client.py

# 3. Confirm nothing else is still conflicted
git status

# 4. Complete the merge
git commit

# If you need to back out entirely before committing:
# git merge --abort
commonMistakes: Leaving conflict marker lines in the file after resolving, which breaks the code
Forgetting to git add the resolved file before committing
Not running git status to confirm every conflicted file has actually been resolved
Not knowing git merge --abort exists as a clean way to back out mid-conflict
keyPoints: Conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) must all be removed after manually resolving
git add stages the resolved file; git status confirms nothing else remains conflicted
git commit completes the merge once all conflicts are resolved
git merge --abort cleanly backs out of an in-progress merge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes identifying and resolving conflict markers
Correctly includes git add and git status in the workflow
Correctly completes the merge with git commit
Mentions git merge --abort as a fallback

questions.title: Writing a basic GitHub Actions workflow to run tests
questions.prompt: Write a basic GitHub Actions YAML workflow that runs a Python project's test suite automatically on every push.
questions.modelAnswer: A minimal CI workflow lives in .github/workflows/ as a YAML file, declaring a name, the on trigger (push, and typically pull_request too), and a jobs section with at least one job that runs on a specified runner image, checks out the repository code (actions/checkout), sets up the correct language runtime (actions/setup-python with a specified version), installs dependencies (commonly from requirements.txt), and finally runs the test command (e.g. pytest). Each of these is a separate step, run in order, and if any step fails the workflow run is marked failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The skeleton I reach for every time has the same shape: trigger on push (and I'd normally add pull_request too, though the question only asked for push), one job targeting ubuntu-latest, and then steps in order -- checkout the repo with actions/checkout, set up the right Python version with actions/setup-python, install dependencies from requirements.txt, and finally run pytest. The thing that trips people up on a first attempt is forgetting the checkout step entirely, since without it the runner has no code to actually test.
questions.example:
name: Run Tests

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest
commonMistakes: Forgetting the actions/checkout step, leaving the runner with no code to test
Omitting a Python version in setup-python, relying on an unpredictable default
Not installing dependencies before running tests
Placing the workflow file outside the required .github/workflows/ directory
keyPoints: Workflow files live in .github/workflows/ and declare on: triggers and jobs
actions/checkout is required to give the runner access to the repository code
actions/setup-python with a pinned version sets up the correct runtime
Steps run in order: checkout, setup, install dependencies, run tests

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct on: trigger and job structure
Includes checkout and setup-python steps correctly
Installs dependencies before running tests
Valid YAML that would actually run

questions.title: Finding and Stopping a Runaway Process From the Command Line
questions.prompt: Write the Linux commands you'd use to find a process by name (say, a hung `node` process), confirm it's actually the right one, and stop it -- first gracefully, then forcibly if it doesn't respond.
questions.modelAnswer: Use pgrep/ps with grep to find PIDs matching the name, inspect the output (full command line, CPU/memory, start time) to confirm it's the right process rather than a false match, send SIGTERM first via kill <pid> and give it a moment to exit cleanly, then only escalate to kill -9 <pid> (SIGKILL) if it's still running, since that's an unconditional immediate termination with no chance for cleanup.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never jump straight to the nuclear option. First I find the candidates with ps aux | grep, being careful to exclude the grep process itself from matching its own search term, or I just use pgrep -a which does that for me and shows the full command line so I can actually confirm it's the right process before touching it. Then I send a plain kill, which is SIGTERM by default, and give it a few seconds to actually exit on its own -- a well-behaved process gets a chance to clean up. Only if it's still sitting there after that do I reach for kill -9, because that's SIGKILL, no cleanup, no second chances, and I want that to be the last resort, not the first move.
questions.example:
# Find candidate processes
ps aux | grep '[n]ode'
# or
pgrep -a node

# Confirm the right PID, then ask it to terminate gracefully
kill 18233

# Give it a few seconds, check it actually stopped
ps -p 18233

# Only if it's still alive, force it
kill -9 18233
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to kill -9 instead of trying a graceful SIGTERM first
Using grep node without excluding the grep process itself from matching (missing the [n] trick or --exclude)
Not verifying the PID actually matches the intended process before killing it
Assuming kill always means SIGKILL, when the plain command sends SIGTERM by default
keyPoints: pgrep/ps with grep locates candidate PIDs; always confirm before killing
Plain kill sends SIGTERM by default, giving the process a chance to clean up
kill -9 sends SIGKILL, an unconditional and uncatchable termination
Escalate to SIGKILL only after confirming the process didn't respond to SIGTERM

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly finds and confirms the target process
Correctly uses kill (SIGTERM) first
Correctly escalates to kill -9 only if needed
Commands are valid and would actually work

questions.title: Setting Up Key-Based SSH Access to a New Server
questions.prompt: Write the commands you'd run to generate a new SSH key pair and set up key-based login to a remote server at 203.0.113.10 for user deploy, so password authentication is no longer needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Generate a new key pair with ssh-keygen (specifying a modern algorithm like ed25519 and ideally a passphrase), then copy the public key to the server's authorized_keys for that user with ssh-copy-id (which handles creating ~/.ssh and setting correct permissions on the remote side), then verify the key-based login actually works before considering disabling password auth on the server.
questions.professionalAnswer: I start by generating a fresh key pair locally with ssh-keygen, using ed25519 rather than the older rsa default and giving it a passphrase if it's for anything beyond a throwaway lab box. Then ssh-copy-id does the actual work of getting the public key onto the server -- it appends it to the right user's authorized_keys and sets the correct permissions on ~/.ssh and the file itself, which matters because sshd will silently refuse a key if those permissions are too open. Before I'd even think about disabling password auth on that server, I log in with the key explicitly to confirm it actually works -- skipping that step and disabling passwords first is how people lock themselves out.
questions.example:
# Generate a new ed25519 key pair with a passphrase
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "deploy-key" -f ~/.ssh/deploy_key

# Copy the public key to the remote server's authorized_keys
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key.pub deploy@203.0.113.10

# Verify key-based login works before disabling passwords
ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key deploy@203.0.113.10
commonMistakes: Copying the private key instead of the public key to the server
Not verifying the key-based login actually works before disabling password auth
Leaving ~/.ssh or authorized_keys with overly open permissions, which sshd will reject
Skipping a passphrase on a key used for anything beyond a throwaway lab environment
keyPoints: ssh-keygen generates a public/private key pair locally
ssh-copy-id installs the public key into the remote user's authorized_keys with correct permissions
Only the public key is ever copied to the server; the private key stays local
Key-based login should be verified working before password authentication is disabled

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly generates the key pair
Correctly copies only the public key to the server
Verifies login before disabling passwords
Commands are valid and in a sensible order

questions.title: Calling an Internal API With a Token From an Environment Variable
questions.prompt: Write a Python script that reads an API token from an environment variable, calls a REST API's GET endpoint with that token as a Bearer auth header, and safely extracts a field from the JSON response -- handling a missing environment variable and a non-200 response.
questions.modelAnswer: Use os.environ.get to read the token with no silent default (raise a clear error if it's missing rather than sending a request with an empty/None token), pass it as an Authorization: Bearer header via requests.get, check response.status_code or use raise_for_status() before trying to parse the body, and access the needed field from response.json() defensively (using .get() rather than direct key indexing) to avoid an unhandled KeyError if the response shape is unexpected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never let a missing token slide quietly into the request -- I read it with os.environ.get, and if it's not set, I exit immediately with a clear message rather than sending a request with a blank Authorization header that would just fail further downstream with a less obvious error. Once I have the token, it goes in as a Bearer token in the Authorization header, and before I touch the response body at all, I call raise_for_status() so a 4xx or 5xx fails loudly right there instead of silently falling through to a .json() call on an error page. And when I do pull a field out of the parsed JSON, I use .get() instead of direct indexing, because trusting an external API's response shape with square brackets is exactly how a KeyError ends up crashing something in production.
questions.example:
import os
import sys
import requests

token = os.environ.get("API_TOKEN")
if not token:
    sys.exit("API_TOKEN environment variable is not set")

response = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/status",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
    timeout=10,
)

try:
    response.raise_for_status()
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    sys.exit(f"API call failed: {e}")

data = response.json()
status = data.get("status")
if status is None:
    sys.exit("Unexpected response shape: 'status' field missing")

print(f"Current status: {status}")
commonMistakes: Not checking whether the environment variable is actually set before using it
Hardcoding the token instead of reading it from the environment
Assuming the response is always 200 and skipping error checking
Using direct dict indexing on the JSON response instead of .get(), risking a KeyError
keyPoints: os.environ.get with an explicit missing-value check, not a silent default, for a required token
Bearer token passed via the Authorization header, not as a query parameter
raise_for_status() or an explicit status check before trusting the response body
Defensive .get() access on the parsed JSON rather than direct key indexing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads and validates the environment variable
Correctly constructs the authenticated request
Correctly checks the response status before parsing
Safely extracts the JSON field with defensive access

questions.title: Reading a Value Out of a YAML Config File in Python
questions.prompt: Write Python code that loads a YAML configuration file and safely reads a nested value (say, `database.host`), handling the case where the file is missing or the key path doesn't exist.
questions.modelAnswer: Use PyYAML's yaml.safe_load (not yaml.load, which can execute arbitrary Python objects from untrusted YAML) to parse the file, wrap the file open in a try/except for FileNotFoundError, and walk the nested dict defensively with .get() chained calls (or a small helper) rather than direct key indexing, so a missing key raises a clear, specific error message instead of an unhandled KeyError or TypeError.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first non-negotiable for me is yaml.safe_load, never yaml.load -- the plain load function can be tricked into constructing arbitrary Python objects from a crafted YAML file, which is a real risk on anything that isn't 100% trusted input. Past that, I wrap the file open specifically for FileNotFoundError so a missing config fails with a message that actually names the problem, and I walk nested keys with chained .get() calls instead of square-bracket indexing, because a missing 'database' section with direct indexing throws a KeyError that doesn't say what's actually missing. If a required key truly isn't there after all that, I exit with a message that names the exact key path, not a generic 'something went wrong.'
commonMistakes: Using yaml.load instead of yaml.safe_load, which can execute arbitrary objects from untrusted YAML
Not handling FileNotFoundError for a missing config file
Using direct key indexing on nested dicts instead of .get(), causing a KeyError on a missing section
Not handling malformed YAML (a YAMLError) separately from a missing file
keyPoints: yaml.safe_load avoids the arbitrary-object-execution risk of yaml.load on untrusted input
FileNotFoundError and YAMLError should both be handled with clear error messages
Nested key access should use .get() chains to avoid unhandled KeyError/TypeError
A missing required key should fail with a specific, actionable message

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load
Handles a missing file clearly
Safely accesses the nested key path
Gives a clear, specific error on a missing key

questions.title: Writing a Production-Reasonable Dockerfile for a Python App
questions.prompt: Write a Dockerfile for a small Python Flask app that installs dependencies from requirements.txt, runs as a non-root user, and keeps the final image reasonably small.
questions.modelAnswer: Use a slim official Python base image, copy and install requirements.txt before copying the rest of the application code (so dependency layers are cached and only rebuilt when requirements.txt actually changes, not on every code edit), create and switch to a dedicated non-root user before running the app, and set an explicit CMD/ENTRYPOINT to launch it -- combining these addresses size (slim base, minimal layers), caching efficiency (requirements copied first), and basic security (non-root).
questions.professionalAnswer: I always copy requirements.txt in and run pip install before copying the rest of the application code -- that ordering means Docker's layer cache only has to rebuild the dependency layer when requirements.txt itself actually changes, not every time I edit a line of app code, which makes a real difference to build times once the project grows. I start from a slim base image rather than the full one to keep the final size down, and before the CMD runs, I create a dedicated non-root user and switch to it with USER, because running as root inside the container is a default I don't want to leave unexamined. --no-cache-dir on the pip install is a small thing but it keeps pip's download cache from bloating the image for no reason.
questions.example:
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
commonMistakes: Copying the entire application before installing dependencies, breaking layer caching on every code change
Running the container as root with no USER directive
Using a full, non-slim base image unnecessarily bloating the final size
Leaving pip's download cache in the image instead of using --no-cache-dir
keyPoints: Copying requirements.txt and installing dependencies before copying the rest of the code preserves layer caching
A dedicated USER directive avoids running the container as root
A slim base image and --no-cache-dir keep the final image smaller
CMD specifies the actual command that runs when the container starts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dependency-install-before-code-copy ordering for caching
Includes a non-root USER directive
Uses a reasonably minimal base image
Valid Dockerfile syntax that would actually build

questions.title: Writing a Docker Compose File for an App and Its Database
questions.prompt: Write a docker-compose.yml that runs a web app (built from a local Dockerfile) alongside a PostgreSQL database, with the app's database connection details passed in as environment variables and the database's data persisted in a named volume.
questions.modelAnswer: Define two services under the services key: the app service built from the local context exposing its port and setting environment variables that reference the db service by its Compose service name (which resolves automatically on Compose's default network) rather than a hardcoded IP; the db service using the official postgres image, its own required environment variables (user/password/db name), and a named volume mapped to Postgres's data directory so data survives container recreation. depends_on expresses that the app should start after the db service.
questions.professionalAnswer: The app service builds from the local Dockerfile and gets its DB connection settings as plain environment variables, but critically, the host it connects to is just the literal service name 'db' -- Compose resolves that automatically on the default network, so there's no hardcoded IP anywhere to go stale. The db service runs the official postgres image with its own required env vars for the user, password, and database name, and I map a named volume onto Postgres's data directory specifically so a docker compose down and back up doesn't wipe the data -- without that volume, recreating the container means recreating an empty database. depends_on just tells Compose to start the app after the db container starts, though I'd note that only covers 'the container is running,' not 'Postgres is actually ready to accept connections yet,' which the app's own retry logic should still handle.
questions.example:
version: "3.9"
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_USER: appuser
      DB_PASSWORD: apppassword
      DB_NAME: appdb
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: apppassword
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db_data:
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the database's container IP instead of using the service name
Not persisting the database's data in a named volume, losing data on container recreation
Omitting depends_on, risking the app starting before the database is ready
Putting real production credentials directly in a committed compose file
keyPoints: Services reach each other by Compose service name on the default network, not by hardcoded IP
A named volume persists the database's data directory across container recreation
depends_on expresses startup ordering between services
Environment variables configure both the app's DB connection and Postgres's own setup

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines both services with appropriate config
Correctly uses service name for DB connection, not an IP
Correctly persists database data with a named volume
Valid Compose YAML that would actually run

questions.title: Writing a Kubernetes Deployment With Resource Limits
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes Deployment manifest that runs 3 replicas of an nginx container, with CPU and memory requests and limits set so a misbehaving Pod can't starve the rest of the node.
questions.modelAnswer: A Deployment manifest needs apiVersion, kind, metadata.name, and a spec with replicas: 3, a selector matching the Pod template's labels, and the Pod template itself specifying the container image and a resources block with both requests (what the scheduler guarantees is available, used for placement decisions) and limits (the hard ceiling the container can't exceed at runtime) for both cpu and memory.
questions.professionalAnswer: The structure is apiVersion, kind: Deployment, then a spec with replicas: 3, a selector that has to exactly match the labels on the Pod template below it -- that mismatch is a surprisingly common way to get a Deployment that silently applies but doesn't do what you expect. Inside the container spec, I set both requests and limits, and I keep straight what each one actually does: requests is what the scheduler uses to decide which node has room for this Pod, limits is the hard ceiling the container can't exceed once it's running. Setting both is what actually protects the rest of the node -- without limits, one container that starts leaking memory can quietly starve everything else scheduled alongside it.
questions.example:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.25
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "256Mi"
commonMistakes: Mismatched selector.matchLabels and template.metadata.labels, making the Deployment invalid
Setting limits without requests, or vice versa, when both serve different purposes
Omitting resource limits entirely, letting one Pod starve the rest of the node
Confusing requests (scheduling guarantee) with limits (runtime ceiling)
keyPoints: selector.matchLabels must exactly match the Pod template's labels
requests inform scheduling decisions; limits are the runtime ceiling a container can't exceed
Setting both requests and limits protects node resources from a single misbehaving Pod
replicas: 3 and the Pod template together define the desired state the Deployment maintains

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Deployment structure with matching selector/labels
Correctly sets replicas to 3
Correctly defines both requests and limits for cpu and memory
Valid YAML that would actually apply

questions.title: Exposing a Deployment With a Service and Ingress
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes Service (ClusterIP) and Ingress that together expose a Deployment's Pods (labeled app: web, listening on port 8080) at the path /app on a given hostname.
questions.modelAnswer: The Service selects Pods by label (app: web) and defines a port mapping (the Service's own port to the container's targetPort 8080), giving those Pods one stable internal ClusterIP and DNS name regardless of which actual Pods are running. The Ingress then routes external HTTP traffic for a specific host and path to that Service by name and port, requiring an Ingress controller actually running in the cluster to do anything -- the Ingress object itself is just a routing rule, not a working load balancer on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: The Service is the easy part -- select on app: web, map port 80 on the Service to targetPort 8080 where the container actually listens, and that gives those Pods one stable ClusterIP and DNS name no matter how many Pods come and go behind it. The Ingress sits on top of that and says 'traffic for this host and this path should go to that Service,' but it's worth being clear that the Ingress object by itself does nothing -- it's a routing rule that only takes effect because an Ingress controller is actually running in the cluster watching for these objects and configuring a real load balancer or proxy accordingly. I've seen people write a perfectly correct Ingress manifest and get confused when nothing happens, simply because no controller was installed to act on it.
questions.example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /app
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web-service
                port:
                  number: 80
commonMistakes: Service selector not matching the Deployment's Pod labels, routing to nothing
Confusing the Service's port with the container's targetPort
Assuming an Ingress object works without an Ingress controller actually running in the cluster
Using ClusterIP and expecting it to be reachable from outside the cluster without the Ingress
keyPoints: The Service selects Pods by label and gives them a stable internal ClusterIP/DNS name
targetPort must match the container's actual listening port, distinct from the Service's own port
The Ingress routes external host/path traffic to a Service by name
An Ingress controller must be running in the cluster for the Ingress object to actually do anything

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Service with matching selector and port mapping
Correct Ingress routing host/path to the Service
Notes the Ingress controller dependency
Valid YAML that would actually apply

questions.title: Mounting a ConfigMap as Environment Variables in a Pod
questions.prompt: Write a ConfigMap holding two application settings and a Pod spec that injects those settings into the container as environment variables.
questions.modelAnswer: Define a ConfigMap with a data section of plain key-value pairs, then in the Pod's container spec use envFrom with a configMapRef pointing to that ConfigMap's name to inject every key as an environment variable automatically, or use individual env entries with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef for selective injection of specific keys under specific variable names -- envFrom is simpler when you want everything, configMapKeyRef when you need to rename or cherry-pick.
questions.professionalAnswer: The ConfigMap itself is just a data block of plain key-value settings. To get those into the container, envFrom with a configMapRef is the simplest route when I want every key injected as an environment variable with the same name -- it's one block, no per-variable wiring. If I only need a subset, or need to rename a key to a different environment variable name than the ConfigMap key itself, I'd use individual env entries with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef instead. One thing worth flagging: editing the ConfigMap afterward doesn't magically update the environment of a Pod that's already running with envFrom -- environment variables are set once at container start, so picking up a config change means rolling the Pod, not just editing the ConfigMap and waiting.
questions.example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_FLAG_X: "enabled"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
commonMistakes: Confusing envFrom (inject everything) with individual configMapKeyRef entries (selective)
Expecting a running Pod's environment to update automatically after editing the ConfigMap
Putting sensitive values in a ConfigMap instead of a Secret
Mismatching the ConfigMap's metadata.name with the name referenced in configMapRef
keyPoints: A ConfigMap's data section holds plain key-value configuration
envFrom with configMapRef injects every key as an environment variable automatically
configMapKeyRef allows selecting and renaming individual keys instead
Pods don't automatically pick up ConfigMap changes; a new rollout is required

Correctly injects it via envFrom/configMapRef
Metadata names correctly linked between objects
Valid YAML that would actually apply

questions.title: A GitHub Actions Workflow With Build, Test, and Artifact Upload Stages
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that, on every push, installs dependencies, runs the test suite, builds a deployable artifact (a zip of the app directory), and uploads that artifact so it's available after the workflow finishes.
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow needs the usual checkout and dependency setup steps, a step that runs the test suite and fails the job if tests fail (stopping the pipeline before producing a build), a build step that packages the app directory, and finally actions/upload-artifact pointed at the packaged output -- artifacts uploaded this way are attached to that specific workflow run and downloadable from the Actions UI or by a later job/workflow, which is distinct from pushing to an actual artifact repository or deploying anywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: The order here matters as much as the steps themselves -- tests have to run and actually gate the job before I package anything, because if a step fails, GitHub Actions stops the job right there and the package/upload steps after it never run, which is exactly the safety net I want against shipping a broken build. Once tests pass, I zip up the app directory and hand it to actions/upload-artifact, which attaches that zip to this specific workflow run so it's downloadable from the Actions UI afterward, or consumable by a later job in the same workflow. I'd be careful not to conflate that with an actual deployment or a push to a real artifact repository -- this is just making the build output available after the run, nothing more.
questions.example:
name: Build and Test

on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:

questions.title: You accidentally committed an API key
questions.prompt: You realize you just pushed a commit containing a real API key in a config file to a shared GitHub repository. Walk through exactly what you'd do, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: The single most important and time-sensitive step is revoking/rotating the actual API key at the provider immediately, before doing anything else with git -- the key is compromised the moment it's pushed, regardless of what happens to the repository afterward, since it may already be visible to anyone with access or to any automated secret-scanning bot watching public repos. Only after the key is dead does cleaning up the repository matter: simply deleting the file in a new commit or using git revert is not sufficient, because the key remains fully visible in the git history of the earlier commit; actually removing it from history requires rewriting history (tools like git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner) and force-pushing the cleaned history, which requires coordinating with any collaborators who may have already pulled the exposed commit. Going forward, the prevention is adding the config file (or a .env pattern) to .gitignore and using a secrets-management approach (environment variables, a secrets manager) instead of committing credentials into any file at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The very first thing I do, before touching git at all, is go revoke and rotate that key at the provider. That has to happen immediately, because the moment it was pushed it's compromised -- it doesn't matter yet whether I clean up the repo, because the actual exposure already happened and the key needs to stop being valid right now. Only after that's done do I worry about the repository itself, and I'm clear with myself that just deleting the file in a new commit or reverting doesn't actually fix anything -- the key is still sitting in the history of that earlier commit for anyone to find. Actually removing it means rewriting history with something like git filter-repo and force-pushing the result, and since that rewrites shared history, I'd give anyone else working on the repo a heads-up before doing it, because their local clones will now be out of sync with the rewritten history. And longer term, I make sure that config file is in .gitignore and that real secrets live in environment variables or an actual secrets manager, not in a file that can be committed in the first place.

Rotating the key only after trying to clean up history, instead of immediately
Not checking whether the repository is public or who else may have already pulled or seen the commit
Rewriting shared history without coordinating with collaborators who may have already pulled it

Rewriting shared history requires coordinating with collaborators, and prevention means never committing secrets at all

questions.title: Tests pass locally but fail only in CI
questions.prompt: Your test suite passes every time on your own machine, but the same tests fail consistently in GitHub Actions. How would you troubleshoot this?
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most common suspect is an environment difference: check that the CI workflow pins the exact same language/runtime version used locally, since a default or different version can change behavior; check whether all dependencies are actually declared (a package installed locally by hand, outside requirements.txt, works locally but is missing in the clean CI environment, which installs strictly from the declared dependency file). The next suspect is state that exists locally but not in CI's clean environment -- a local environment variable, config file, or cached data the tests implicitly depend on but that was never committed or set in the workflow's env. Reading the actual CI failure logs carefully (not just 'it failed') almost always shows which of these it is -- a missing module error points to dependencies, an authentication or config error points to missing environment variables or secrets, and a different error entirely can point to a version mismatch.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct here is that CI is actually telling me the truth and my local machine is the one with hidden, undeclared state -- CI runs from a clean environment every time, so if something only works locally, it's relying on something that exists on my machine but was never actually captured in the repo or the workflow config. First thing I do is actually read the CI failure log carefully rather than just seeing 'failed' and guessing -- a ModuleNotFoundError usually means something I have installed locally never made it into requirements.txt, an auth or config-related error usually means an environment variable or secret I have set locally isn't configured in the GitHub Actions workflow, and a totally different error can point to a Python version mismatch between my machine and whatever the workflow specifies. I treat 'works for me, fails in CI' as the environment being the bug, not the test, and the fix is almost always making the CI environment's actual dependencies and config match what my code genuinely needs, not special-casing CI to work around it.

Not reading the actual CI failure logs in detail before guessing at a cause
Having dependencies installed locally that were never added to requirements.txt
Relying on local environment variables, config files, or cached state that CI's clean environment doesn't have

Missing environment variables/secrets in the CI workflow configuration are another common cause

questions.title: A systemd Service Fails to Start — How Do You Actually Diagnose It
questions.prompt: You run `systemctl start myapp` and it fails immediately with no useful output in the terminal. Walk through exactly how you'd find out why.
questions.modelAnswer: Start with systemctl status myapp, which shows the service's current state, the most recent log lines, and the exact exit code of the last attempt -- that alone often points straight at the problem (e.g. 'exit code 203/EXEC' means the ExecStart path is wrong or not executable). If that's not enough, pull the full logs for just that unit with journalctl -u myapp (and -xe for extra context on the most recent boot), which shows everything the service itself printed to stdout/stderr plus systemd's own messages about it, since systemd captures that output by default rather than it going to the terminal that ran systemctl start. Common root causes to check specifically: the ExecStart binary path is wrong or lacks execute permission, a required environment variable the unit file doesn't set is missing, or the working directory/user specified in the unit file doesn't have access to something the app needs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never try to guess from the terminal output alone, because systemctl start usually gives you almost nothing there -- systemd captures the service's actual stdout/stderr itself, it doesn't just print it back to you. So the first real step is systemctl status myapp, which shows the current state, the last few log lines, and critically the exit code from the last attempt -- something like exit code 203/EXEC tells me immediately that the ExecStart path is wrong or isn't executable, without needing to dig further. If I need more context than that, journalctl -u myapp pulls the full log history for just that unit, which is where the application's own error output usually is. From there I'm specifically checking three things: is the ExecStart path actually correct and executable, does the unit file set every environment variable the app actually needs, and does the user/working directory specified in the unit file have access to whatever the app is trying to touch.
commonMistakes: Only looking at the terminal's immediate output instead of journalctl -u for the full captured logs
Not checking the specific exit code systemctl status reports, which often names the exact failure category
Assuming the problem is the application code without checking unit file issues (bad path, missing permission)
Not checking whether required environment variables are actually set in the unit file

questions.title: SSH Says 'Permission Denied (publickey)' — Where Do You Actually Look
questions.prompt: You try to SSH into a server using a key you know is correct, and you get 'Permission denied (publickey)'. Walk through the specific things you'd check, in order, to find the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: Run the connection with verbose output (ssh -v, or -vvv for more detail) first, since it shows exactly which keys the client offered and whether the server rejected each one, instead of guessing blindly. Then check, in order: that you're actually pointing at the right private key (ssh -i explicitly, or that it's loaded in ssh-agent / referenced correctly in ~/.ssh/config), that the matching public key is actually present in the right user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, and -- a very common and easy-to-miss cause -- that the permissions on the server are correct: ~/.ssh must be 700 and authorized_keys must be 600 (or similarly restrictive), because sshd silently refuses to use a key if the file permissions are too permissive, often without a clearly worded error. Also worth checking: that PubkeyAuthentication is actually enabled in the server's sshd_config.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never guess at this one, because 'Permission denied (publickey)' on its own is nearly useless -- the real diagnosis starts with ssh -v, or -vvv if I need more detail, which actually shows me which key the client offered and how the server responded to it. From there I work down a specific checklist: am I even offering the key I think I am, whether that's via an explicit -i flag, something loaded in ssh-agent, or a Host entry in ~/.ssh/config; is the matching public key actually sitting in the right user's authorized_keys on the server; and -- the one that catches people constantly -- are the permissions on the server actually correct, because sshd will silently refuse to even look at a key if ~/.ssh isn't 700 or authorized_keys isn't 600, and it does this without an error message that clearly says 'your permissions are wrong.' If all of that checks out, I'd also confirm PubkeyAuthentication is actually turned on in sshd_config, since I've seen that disabled on a hardened server.

Assuming the key itself is broken without checking server-side authorized_keys contents
Overlooking file permission requirements on ~/.ssh and authorized_keys as a silent rejection cause
Not checking whether PubkeyAuthentication is actually enabled in sshd_config

Confirm the matching public key is actually present in the server's authorized_keys
Overly permissive ~/.ssh or authorized_keys permissions cause a silent rejection on the server side

Checks authorized_keys content on the server

questions.title: A Script Works When You Run It Manually but Fails Under Cron
questions.prompt: A Python script works perfectly when you run it yourself from the terminal, but the same script fails silently when it runs as a scheduled cron job. What's your diagnostic approach?
questions.modelAnswer: The core insight is that cron runs jobs with a minimal environment, not your interactive shell's environment -- so the most common cause is the script relying on something only present in your personal shell session: a PATH that includes a directory cron's PATH doesn't, an environment variable set in your .bashrc/.profile that cron never sources, or a relative file path that resolves differently because cron's working directory isn't the same as wherever you were when you ran it manually. The fix is making the script's dependencies explicit rather than relying on an interactive shell's state: use absolute paths for any files and binaries the script invokes, explicitly set any required environment variables either in the crontab line itself or by sourcing a specific env file at the top of the script, and -- critically for actually seeing what failed -- redirect the cron job's output to a log file, since cron jobs run with no interactive terminal and failures that would show on your screen manually are otherwise silently discarded.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption is always that cron is the honest one here and my interactive shell is hiding something -- cron runs with a genuinely minimal environment, nothing like the PATH and exported variables my .bashrc sets up for an interactive session. So the usual suspects are a binary the script calls that's only found because of something in my personal PATH, an environment variable I've exported in my shell profile that cron never sources, or a relative path that only resolves correctly because of whatever directory I happened to be sitting in when I ran it by hand. The fix is to stop relying on any of that implicitly -- use absolute paths everywhere in the script, set required environment variables explicitly in the crontab entry itself, and redirect the job's output to a log file, because cron jobs have no terminal to print errors to, so without that redirect a failure just vanishes silently instead of telling me anything.
commonMistakes: Assuming cron runs with the same environment as an interactive shell session
Using relative file paths that depend on an assumed working directory cron doesn't share
Not redirecting the cron job's stdout/stderr to a log file, losing the actual error message
Not checking PATH differences when a cron job can't find a binary that works fine manually

Scripts invoked by cron should use absolute paths rather than assuming a working directory
Required environment variables need to be explicitly set for the cron context, not inherited
Redirecting cron output to a log file is essential, since failures are otherwise silently discarded

Identifies PATH/absolute-path issues specifically

Mentions redirecting output to a log for visibility

questions.title: A Container Starts and Immediately Exits — How Do You Find Out Why
questions.prompt: You run `docker run myapp` and the container exits immediately with no obvious error on screen. How would you actually diagnose this?
questions.modelAnswer: First check docker ps -a (not just docker ps, since the container isn't running anymore) to see its exit code, then pull the actual output with docker logs <container>, since that's where the application's real stdout/stderr -- and the actual reason -- usually is, even if nothing printed to your current terminal. A container exits as soon as its main process (PID 1) exits, so a very common cause is the image's CMD/ENTRYPOINT finishing immediately rather than running a long-lived foreground process (e.g. accidentally running a one-shot script instead of starting a server, or a server that's misconfigured and crashes on startup). If the logs aren't revealing enough, running the image interactively with an overridden entrypoint (docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myapp) lets you poke around inside and try starting the actual command by hand to see the real error.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first mistake people make here is checking docker ps, which shows nothing because the container already exited -- docker ps -a is what actually shows it, along with its exit code, which is already a useful clue. From there, docker logs on that container ID usually has the real story, because whatever the app printed to stdout/stderr on its way out is captured there even though nothing showed on my screen. The underlying mechanic to remember is that a container lives exactly as long as its PID 1 process does, so an instant exit almost always means that process finished or crashed immediately -- a common version of this is accidentally running a one-shot command instead of a long-lived server, or a server that's misconfigured and dies on startup before it ever binds a port. If the logs still aren't telling me enough, I'll run the image interactively with the entrypoint overridden to a shell, and then try launching the real command by hand inside it to see the actual error as it happens.
