Not checking docker logs, missing the actual application error
Assuming a quick exit always means a crash, rather than a one-shot command that simply finished and exited normally
Not trying an interactive shell override to manually run the failing command and see its real output

questions.title: Two Containers Can't Reach Each Other by Name
questions.prompt: Your app container tries to connect to `db:5432` and gets a connection failure, even though both containers are running. What would you check to figure out why the app can't reach the database by that name?
questions.modelAnswer: Docker's built-in name-based DNS resolution only works between containers that are actually attached to the same user-defined network -- it does not work on the legacy default bridge network, and it doesn't work if the containers were started separately without being placed on a shared network at all. So the first check is docker network inspect on whatever network you expect them to share, confirming both containers actually appear in it; if they were started with separate docker run commands with no --network flag, they likely landed on the default bridge, where name resolution doesn't work the way it does on a user-defined network. Beyond networking, also confirm the database container is actually listening on the expected port inside the container (not just that the container is running) and that nothing in the app's own connection string is pointing at the wrong hostname or port.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing people get wrong here is assuming any two running containers can resolve each other by name -- that's only true when they're actually on the same user-defined network. Docker's name-based DNS doesn't work on the legacy default bridge network at all, so if both containers were started with separate docker run commands and no explicit --network flag, there's a real chance they both landed on that default bridge where this just doesn't work. My first move is docker network inspect on whichever network I think they should share, to confirm both containers are actually listed as members of it -- if one's missing, that's the whole problem right there. If the networking checks out, I'd also double-check that the database is actually listening on 5432 inside its own container, not just that the container is technically running, since those are two different questions.

Not checking whether both containers are actually attached to the same user-defined network
Confusing the legacy default bridge network's lack of DNS resolution with a general Docker limitation
Not verifying the target service is actually listening on the expected port before troubleshooting networking

questions.title: Docker Says 'No Space Left on Device' Even Though the Host Has Free Disk
questions.prompt: A `docker build` fails with 'no space left on device,' but `df -h` on the host shows plenty of free space. What's actually going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Docker's images, containers, volumes, and build cache all live in Docker's own storage area, which is often on a different filesystem/partition than wherever df -h is showing free space on the host, or is simply being consumed by accumulated Docker objects that aren't visible in a general disk check -- dangling images, stopped containers, unused volumes, and build cache layers all pile up over time and are a very common cause of this specific error even when the rest of the host clearly has room. The fix is to actually check Docker's own disk usage with docker system df, which breaks down exactly what Docker is holding onto, and then reclaim space with docker system prune (and specifically docker system prune --volumes if unused volumes are a contributor), rather than trying to free space elsewhere on the host that Docker isn't even using.
questions.professionalAnswer: This one trips people up because df -h is answering a different question than the one that actually matters -- it's showing general host disk space, while Docker's images, containers, volumes, and build cache live in Docker's own storage area, which can fill up on its own regardless of what the rest of the host looks like. Instead of chasing disk space elsewhere on the host, I go straight to docker system df, which actually breaks down what Docker itself is holding -- images, containers, local volumes, build cache -- and in my experience, accumulated build cache and dangling images from repeated builds are the usual culprit. The fix is docker system prune, and if unused volumes turn out to be a real contributor, I add --volumes to that, rather than spending time freeing space on the host that Docker was never going to use anyway.

questions.title: A Pod Is Stuck in CrashLoopBackOff — How Do You Diagnose It
questions.prompt: `kubectl get pods` shows a Pod repeatedly cycling through CrashLoopBackOff. Walk through how you'd actually figure out why it keeps crashing.
questions.modelAnswer: CrashLoopBackOff means the container's main process is exiting (crashing or finishing) repeatedly, and Kubernetes is backing off with increasing delay between restart attempts -- it's a symptom, not a specific cause, so the actual diagnosis is: kubectl describe pod <name> to see recent events (which often shows the exact exit code and reason, like OOMKilled for a memory limit being hit), and kubectl logs <name> for the current container's output, plus kubectl logs <name> --previous specifically to see the log output from the crashed instance before it restarted, since by the time you look, the current attempt's logs may be too fresh to show the actual error. Common root causes to check specifically: the app crashing on a missing ConfigMap/Secret value, a failing liveness probe killing an otherwise-working container prematurely, or the container being OOMKilled because its memory limit is set too low for what it actually needs.
questions.professionalAnswer: CrashLoopBackOff is a status, not a diagnosis -- it just tells me the container keeps exiting and Kubernetes keeps backing off before retrying. The actual investigation starts with kubectl describe pod, which surfaces recent events and very often the exact exit reason, like OOMKilled if a memory limit got hit. Then I pull logs, but specifically with --previous as well as the plain kubectl logs, because the current attempt might be too fresh to show anything useful -- the crashed instance's own output, from right before it died, is usually in the previous logs, not the current ones. From there I'm checking a short list of usual suspects: is the app crashing because a ConfigMap or Secret value it expects is missing, is a misconfigured liveness probe killing an otherwise healthy container before it's even finished starting up, or is this genuinely an OOMKill because the memory limit is set tighter than what the app actually needs.

questions.title: A Pod Is Stuck in Pending — What Do You Check
questions.prompt: A Pod you just created stays in `Pending` status and never gets scheduled. What would you check to find out why?
questions.modelAnswer: A Pod stuck in Pending means the scheduler hasn't been able to place it on any node, and kubectl describe pod <name> shows the scheduler's own events explaining exactly why -- this is the right first step rather than guessing. The most common reasons: the Pod's resource requests (cpu/memory) exceed what any single node currently has available, so no node qualifies; a node selector, affinity rule, or taint/toleration mismatch rules out every available node; or a required PersistentVolumeClaim hasn't been bound yet because no matching PersistentVolume or StorageClass provisioner is available. Each of these shows up as a specific, readable message in the describe output (e.g. 'Insufficient cpu' or 'node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate'), so the fix is almost always visible directly in that event text rather than needing deeper investigation.

questions.title: Choosing a branching strategy for a small team shipping weekly
questions.prompt: You're setting up Git workflow conventions for a small team of four engineers shipping an AI product feature-by-feature, roughly weekly. Would you reach for Git Flow or trunk-based development, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: For a small team shipping frequently, trunk-based development is generally the better fit: engineers work off short-lived feature branches that merge back into main quickly (ideally within a day or two), main stays continuously deployable, and there's no long-lived develop or release branch structure to keep in sync. Git Flow's additional branch types (develop, release, hotfix, feature, in parallel) add real process overhead -- extra merge points, longer-lived branches that drift further from main the longer they live, increasing conflict risk -- that make more sense for a team managing multiple release versions in production simultaneously (like versioned software with long-term support branches) than for a small team shipping one continuously deployed product weekly. The actual decision criterion isn't team size alone, it's release cadence and whether multiple versions need active parallel maintenance; trunk-based fits a single continuously shipped product, Git Flow fits multi-version maintenance.
questions.professionalAnswer: For this specific situation, I'd go trunk-based. With four engineers shipping weekly, short-lived feature branches that merge back into main quickly keep main always close to what's actually been built and tested, and there's no develop/release branch structure to keep synchronized, which is pure process overhead this team doesn't need. Git Flow's extra branch types earn their complexity when you genuinely have multiple versions of a product in production at once needing separate maintenance -- think versioned software with long-term support branches -- but for a team shipping one continuously deployed product, that structure just adds more places for things to drift and more merge points where conflicts can pile up the longer a branch lives. My actual decision rule isn't about team size by itself, it's about release cadence and whether there are multiple live versions to maintain in parallel -- and this team has neither, so the lighter-weight trunk-based approach is the better fit.

Not recognizing that Git Flow's extra branch types exist to serve multi-version maintenance needs
Assuming team size alone, rather than release cadence and version-maintenance needs, drives the decision
Not mentioning that longer-lived branches increase merge conflict risk the longer they live

Git Flow's extra branch structure is justified by multi-version parallel maintenance needs

questions.title: Choosing Between a systemd Service and a Cron Job for a Recurring Task
questions.prompt: You need to run a data-cleanup script every night at 2 AM. Would you set it up as a systemd timer/service or a cron job, and what's the actual deciding factor?
questions.modelAnswer: For a simple, periodic task like this, either genuinely works, and the real deciding factor is less about raw capability and more about what visibility and control you need around it: systemd timers integrate with systemd's own logging (journalctl), dependency management (can require another service/target to be active first), and give you the same status/restart tooling as any other systemd-managed service, which matters if this task's reliability needs monitoring alongside everything else running on the box. Cron is simpler to set up and perfectly adequate for a genuinely standalone script with no dependencies and no need for that tooling, and it remains the more universally familiar option across different Linux environments. The deciding factor in practice is whether the task needs to integrate with the rest of the system's service management and logging (favoring a systemd timer) or whether it's truly simple and standalone (favoring cron, where simplicity itself is the advantage).
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, either tool can run a script at 2 AM reliably, so I don't treat this as a capability question -- it's a tooling-integration question. If this cleanup script's reliability actually matters enough that I want its logs in journalctl alongside everything else, or I want it to depend on another service being up first, or I want the same systemctl status visibility I get on every other service on the box, a systemd timer earns its slightly higher setup cost. If it's genuinely a standalone script with no dependencies and nobody's going to lose sleep over checking on it beyond a basic log file, cron is simpler, more universally understood, and doesn't need the extra ceremony. So my actual decision isn't about which one 'can' schedule a task -- they both can -- it's about whether I want this task to live inside systemd's management and logging, or stay simple and separate.

Not mentioning systemd timers' integration with journalctl logging and service dependencies
Defaulting to cron purely out of habit without considering whether better tooling integration would actually help
Overcomplicating a genuinely simple, standalone task with systemd timer dependency management it doesn't need

Cron is simpler and sufficient for a standalone script with no dependencies on other services
The real deciding factor is whether the task needs system-service integration, not raw scheduling capability

questions.title: When Do You Reach for Python Instead of Bash for an Automation Task
questions.prompt: You need to automate a task that involves calling a REST API, parsing JSON, and making a few conditional decisions based on the response. Would you write it in Bash or Python, and what's the actual reasoning?
questions.modelAnswer: For this specific task, Python is the better fit, and the reasoning isn't 'Python is always better' -- it's that this task's requirements (structured HTTP calls, JSON parsing, and meaningful conditional logic on structured data) are exactly what Bash is weak at and Python is built for: Bash can technically call curl and pipe through tools like jq to extract JSON fields, but that approach gets fragile and hard to read fast once there's real branching logic, proper error handling, or more than a couple of fields to extract, whereas Python's requests library and native dict/JSON handling make the same logic both more robust and more readable. The general rule of thumb: Bash is the right tool for simple, linear sequences of commands and file/text operations (which is genuinely its strength), and Python becomes the better choice once a task needs real data structures, non-trivial conditional logic, or structured error handling -- which is exactly what calling an API and reasoning about its JSON response requires.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this one in Python, but not because I think Python is just generally superior -- it's because this specific task's shape is exactly where Bash starts to struggle. You can technically do an API call and JSON parsing in Bash with curl piped into jq, and for a single field extraction that's fine, but the moment there's real conditional logic branching on a few different fields, that approach gets fragile and genuinely hard to read. Python's requests library and native dict handling make the same logic both more robust and much more legible. My actual rule of thumb is that Bash is great for simple, linear command sequences and file or text operations -- that's genuinely its strength -- but once a task needs real data structures and non-trivial branching, which is exactly what reasoning about a JSON API response requires, Python is the better tool for the job.

Assuming Bash can't call APIs at all, rather than that it gets unwieldy for anything beyond simple cases
Framing the choice as 'Python is always superior' instead of matching the tool to the task's actual shape
Not recognizing Bash's genuine strength for simple linear command sequences and text/file operations

Python's native data structures and libraries (requests, json) handle structured API/JSON work much more robustly
The real decision criterion is the task's shape -- structured data and conditional logic favor Python

questions.title: Single Container vs. a Sidecar: Designing a Container With a Log Shipper
questions.prompt: Your app needs its logs shipped to a centralized logging system. Would you add that log-shipping logic inside the app's own container, or run it as a separate sidecar container alongside it? Walk through the actual tradeoff.
questions.modelAnswer: Running the log shipper as a separate sidecar container -- sharing a volume with the app container so the shipper can read the log files the app writes -- is generally the better design, because it keeps the app container focused on one responsibility (running the app) and lets the log-shipping logic be updated, restarted, or swapped independently without touching the app's own image at all. Baking the shipping logic directly into the app container's image couples two genuinely separate concerns together: an app-code change now requires rebuilding an image that also contains logging logic, and a logging-tool update requires rebuilding and redeploying the app itself even though nothing about the app actually changed. The tradeoff isn't free -- a sidecar means coordinating two containers (sharing a volume, getting their lifecycles aligned) instead of one simple container -- but that coordination overhead is usually worth it for the independence it buys for genuinely separate concerns.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run the log shipper as a sidecar, sharing a volume with the app so it can read whatever log files the app writes. The reason isn't aesthetic -- it's that baking the shipping logic directly into the app's image couples two things that should be able to change independently: an app code change now means rebuilding an image that also happens to contain logging logic, and bumping the logging tool's version means rebuilding and redeploying the app itself even though nothing about the app changed at all. A sidecar keeps those update cycles separate. The real cost is coordination -- now I've got two containers that need a shared volume and lifecycles that are at least loosely aligned, instead of one simple container -- but for something as genuinely separate as log shipping, that coordination overhead is a fair price for not coupling unrelated concerns together.

Forgetting the sidecar needs a shared volume to actually read the app's log files

questions.title: Why Docker Compose Isn't Enough Once You Need Production Reliability
questions.prompt: Your team uses Docker Compose happily for local development. A stakeholder asks why you can't just also use Compose to run the application in production. What's the actual technical answer?
questions.modelAnswer: Compose is explicitly a single-host tool: it defines and runs a multi-container application on one machine, with no concept of scheduling containers across multiple hosts, no automatic self-healing if a container crashes and the host itself has an issue, and no built-in rolling-update or scaling mechanism beyond manually re-running commands. Production reliability requirements -- surviving a single host failure, scaling a specific service horizontally under load, rolling out updates without downtime, automatically rescheduling a failed container onto a healthy node -- are exactly the capabilities a real orchestrator (Kubernetes, or a managed equivalent) provides and Compose fundamentally doesn't, because it was designed to solve local multi-container development and simple single-host deployments, not distributed production operation. The honest answer isn't 'Compose is bad,' it's that Compose and an orchestrator solve genuinely different problems, and production reliability needs the second one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer isn't that Compose is somehow bad -- it's that it was built to solve a different problem than the one production reliability actually requires. Compose runs everything on one host, full stop -- there's no concept of scheduling across multiple machines, so if that one host goes down, the whole application goes down with it. It also has no real self-healing: if a container crashes, Compose doesn't automatically reschedule it onto a healthy machine, because there isn't another machine in the picture at all. And scaling or rolling out an update without downtime means manually re-running commands rather than anything built in. Those three things -- surviving a host failure, automatic rescheduling, and zero-downtime rollouts -- are exactly what a real orchestrator like Kubernetes exists to provide, and that's the actual gap, not a vague sense that Compose is 'less mature.'

Not mentioning Compose's single-host limitation specifically as the core gap
Framing Compose as simply inferior rather than designed for a different problem (local dev, single-host)
Overlooking self-healing/automatic rescheduling as a specific production requirement Compose lacks

questions.title: Deployment vs. StatefulSet: Choosing for a Web App vs. a Database
questions.prompt: Would you run a stateless web app and a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster the same way in Kubernetes -- both as Deployments -- or would you make a different choice for the database? Explain the actual reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer: The stateless web app fits a Deployment well, since its Pods are interchangeable -- any replica can serve any request, Pods can be freely created, destroyed, and replaced in any order with new random names, and nothing about Pod identity matters. A self-managed database cluster needs a StatefulSet instead, because StatefulSet Pods get stable, predictable network identities (pod-0, pod-1, pod-2, not random names) and stable per-Pod storage that follows that specific Pod across rescheduling, both of which matter for a database where each replica might have a distinct role (primary vs. replica) and its own persistent data directory that must stay attached to that specific instance, not get randomly reassigned. Using a Deployment for the database would risk losing the stable identity-to-storage mapping that database replication and recovery logic typically depend on; using a StatefulSet for the stateless web app would just be unnecessary overhead for Pods that don't need any of those guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer: No, I wouldn't treat them the same, and the difference isn't about which one is 'more important' -- it's about whether Pod identity actually matters. The web app's Pods are genuinely interchangeable: any one of them can serve any request, and a Deployment freely creating, killing, and replacing Pods with new random names is exactly fine, because nothing cares which specific Pod answers a given request. The database is the opposite case -- each replica likely has a distinct role, like primary versus replica, and its own persistent data directory that has to stay attached to that specific instance across rescheduling, not get randomly reshuffled. A StatefulSet is what actually gives you that: stable, predictable Pod names like db-0 and db-1, and storage that follows a specific Pod rather than whichever Pod happens to come up next. Running the database as a plain Deployment would risk breaking exactly that identity-to-storage mapping that database replication logic usually depends on.

Not knowing StatefulSet Pods get predictable, stable names rather than random ones
Using a StatefulSet for a genuinely stateless workload that doesn't need per-Pod identity guarantees
Assuming Deployment and StatefulSet are interchangeable with just different names

StatefulSet Pods get stable, predictable names and storage that follow a specific Pod across rescheduling
A database with per-replica roles and persistent state needs that stable identity-to-storage mapping
Using the wrong one either breaks database identity guarantees or adds unneeded overhead for stateless apps

Correctly recommends StatefulSet for the database with sound reasoning

questions.title: Choosing a Kubernetes Service Type for the Right Job
questions.prompt: Kubernetes gives you ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Service types. Walk through when each one is actually the right choice.
questions.modelAnswer: ClusterIP, the default, gives a Service an internal-only address reachable from inside the cluster -- the right choice for internal communication between Pods/services that should never be reached directly from outside, like a backend API only the frontend talks to. NodePort opens a specific port on every node's own IP, making the Service reachable from outside the cluster via any node's address and that port -- useful for simple external access or on-prem/bare-metal setups without a cloud load balancer available, but it ties external access to node IPs directly and isn't the typical production-facing choice on a cloud platform. LoadBalancer provisions an actual external cloud load balancer (on AKS, EKS, etc.) in front of the Service, giving it a real external IP/DNS name managed by the cloud provider -- the standard choice for genuinely internet-facing production traffic on a cloud-managed cluster. In practice, an Ingress is often layered on top of a ClusterIP or LoadBalancer Service to handle host/path-based routing for multiple services behind one external entry point, rather than provisioning a separate LoadBalancer per service.
questions.professionalAnswer: ClusterIP is my default for anything that only needs to be reached from inside the cluster -- a backend API the frontend talks to internally has no business being reachable from outside at all, so ClusterIP is the right scope. NodePort opens a specific port on every node's own IP, which is genuinely useful on bare-metal or on-prem clusters with no cloud load balancer available, but on a cloud platform it's rarely my production choice, since it ties external access directly to node IPs rather than anything more stable. LoadBalancer is what I reach for when something genuinely needs to be internet-facing on a cloud-managed cluster -- it provisions a real external load balancer through the cloud provider, with its own IP or DNS name. In practice, I usually don't provision one LoadBalancer per service -- I'll put an Ingress on top of ClusterIP services and route multiple services through a single external entry point, which is more efficient than a separate cloud load balancer for every single service.

Not mentioning Ingress as the typical layer on top for routing multiple services behind one entry point

NodePort exposes a port on every node directly, useful for simple/bare-metal external access
LoadBalancer provisions a real cloud load balancer, the standard for production external traffic on a cloud cluster
Ingress typically layers on top of ClusterIP/LoadBalancer for host/path routing across multiple services

Correctly explains LoadBalancer's use case

questions.title: Designing Config So the Same Manifests Work Across Dev, Staging, and Prod
questions.prompt: You want the exact same Deployment manifest to work in dev, staging, and production, with only the configuration values (database host, feature flags, API keys) differing per environment. How would you actually structure your ConfigMaps and Secrets to make that work?
questions.modelAnswer: The Deployment manifest itself should reference ConfigMap and Secret names generically (via envFrom or individual env entries) rather than hardcoding any environment-specific values directly in the Pod spec -- the actual values live entirely in the ConfigMap/Secret objects, not the Deployment. Each environment then gets its own ConfigMap and Secret (same keys, different values), typically isolated in separate namespaces or separate clusters per environment, so the identical Deployment YAML can be applied to any environment unchanged, picking up whichever environment's ConfigMap/Secret happens to exist there under the same referenced name. This is commonly layered with a templating or overlay tool (like Kustomize or Helm) specifically so the base Deployment definition stays truly identical across environments while only small, explicit overlay files vary the config values and resource sizing per environment, rather than maintaining three nearly-duplicate copies of the full manifest.
questions.professionalAnswer: The Deployment itself should never know it's running in dev versus prod -- it just references a ConfigMap and a Secret by name, generically, and the actual values live entirely in those separate objects, not baked into the Pod spec. Each environment gets its own ConfigMap and Secret with the same keys but different values, and I'd isolate those by namespace or by cluster per environment so the identical Deployment YAML can be applied anywhere unchanged and just pick up whatever's actually sitting in that environment under the referenced name. In practice I wouldn't hand-maintain three almost-identical copies of the full manifest for this -- I'd use something like Kustomize or Helm, where the base Deployment definition stays genuinely shared and only small, explicit overlay files vary the config values and resource sizing per environment.

Not considering a templating/overlay tool (Kustomize, Helm) to keep the base manifest truly shared

questions.title: Designing an Environment Promotion Flow With Approvals
questions.prompt: You're designing a CI/CD pipeline that promotes a build through dev, staging, and production. Walk through how you'd structure the promotion flow and where you'd actually put approval gates.
questions.modelAnswer: The core principle is building the deployable artifact exactly once and promoting that same artifact through each environment unchanged, rather than rebuilding separately for each environment -- rebuilding per environment risks subtle differences (dependency versions, build-time config) sneaking in between what was actually tested and what gets deployed to production, defeating the purpose of testing at all. Deployment to dev typically happens automatically on every successful build/test, since dev is low-risk and fast feedback matters most there; staging usually gets either automatic promotion or a lightweight approval, since it's meant to validate the build under more production-like conditions before the real gate; production is where a deliberate, explicit human approval gate belongs, specifically because that's the step with real business/customer consequences if something's wrong, and that gate should require a specific person or role to actively approve, not just elapse automatically. The approval gates get stricter as risk increases, not uniformly applied at every stage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The principle I design around is build once, promote many times -- the exact artifact that got tested is the exact artifact that goes to production, never a fresh rebuild per environment, because rebuilding separately risks some subtle difference -- a dependency version, a build-time flag -- sneaking in between what was actually validated and what ships, which quietly defeats the point of testing at all. From there, I scale the approval friction to the actual risk: dev deploys automatically on every passing build, because fast feedback matters more there than ceremony; staging either promotes automatically or gets a lightweight approval, since its job is validating under more realistic conditions before the real gate; and production gets a deliberate, explicit approval from a specific person or role, because that's the step with actual business consequences if something's wrong. I don't apply the same heavy gate everywhere -- that just slows down low-risk stages without adding real safety, while under-protecting the one stage that actually needs it.

Not recognizing that staging's purpose is validating under more production-like conditions before the real gate

questions.title: Choosing Between GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps Pipelines
questions.prompt: A company is deciding between GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps Pipelines for their CI/CD. What would actually drive that decision, beyond just 'which one do we already know'?
questions.modelAnswer: The real driver is usually where the rest of the organization's tooling already lives and how deep the integration needs to be: if the codebase is already on GitHub, GitHub Actions keeps workflows defined right alongside the code with the tightest possible integration (PR checks, status badges, the same permissions model), while Azure DevOps Pipelines makes more sense when the organization is already invested in the broader Azure DevOps suite -- Boards for work tracking, Repos, Artifacts -- or has deep ties to Azure-specific deployment targets and service connections that Azure DevOps handles natively. Beyond tooling fit, practical factors include existing licensing/cost structure (Azure DevOps often comes bundled into existing Microsoft/Azure enterprise agreements), the team's existing familiarity (not as the deciding factor alone, but a real cost to ignore), and whether the organization needs on-premises self-hosted agents with specific network access, which both platforms support but with different setup models. The decision should follow where the organization's source code, work tracking, and deployment targets already live, not an abstract feature comparison.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't run this as a pure feature checklist, because both platforms can do the core job -- build, test, deploy. The real question is where everything else already lives. If the code's already on GitHub, Actions keeps the workflow definitions right next to the code with the tightest integration into PRs and the same permissions model, and that's a real, ongoing convenience. If the org's already deep into the Azure DevOps suite -- Boards for tracking work, Repos, Artifacts -- or has a lot of Azure-specific deployment targets that Azure DevOps handles natively through service connections, that existing investment is a strong pull the other way. Beyond that, I'd check whether the company already has a Microsoft enterprise agreement that bundles Azure DevOps in a way that changes the actual cost comparison, and I wouldn't dismiss team familiarity either -- it's not the deciding factor by itself, but it's a real cost if I ignore it entirely.

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.

Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision

Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a methodical, logically ordered investigation
Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Receiving a harsh code review comment
questions.prompt: A senior engineer leaves a blunt review comment on your pull request: 'This whole approach is wrong, rewrite it.' No further explanation. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't respond defensively or silently rewrite the whole thing based on a comment that doesn't actually explain the problem -- it asks a specific, concrete follow-up question that gets at the missing information: what specifically is wrong with the approach, and what alternative would they suggest instead. The point isn't to challenge the reviewer's judgment or to litigate whether the comment was rude; it's that 'rewrite it' without a reason isn't actionable, and building the wrong thing a second time because the actual objection was never understood wastes both people's time. A strong answer also recognizes that terse review comments are common under time pressure and don't necessarily reflect anything personal, so the response should stay professional and curious rather than escalating the tone.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move isn't to get defensive or to just start rewriting blindly based on a comment that doesn't actually tell me what's wrong -- it's to ask a direct, specific question: 'Can you point to what specifically is the problem here, or suggest the direction you'd want instead?' I'm not trying to push back on the feedback itself, I genuinely can't act on 'this is wrong' without knowing what 'wrong' means, and guessing wrong a second time wastes both our time. I also don't read too much into the tone -- a terse comment under time pressure usually isn't personal, and matching that terseness with defensiveness of my own doesn't get me the information I actually need to fix the thing correctly.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or arguing about the tone of the comment instead of seeking the missing information
Silently rewriting the code based on a guess about what the reviewer meant, without clarifying first
Escalating the interaction's tone instead of staying professional and specific
Taking a terse comment as a personal attack rather than asking a direct clarifying question
keyPoints: An unactionable review comment should be met with a specific clarifying question, not a guess or defensiveness
The goal is understanding the actual objection, not litigating the comment's tone
Guessing wrong a second time wastes both the reviewer's and the author's time
Staying professional and curious, rather than escalating tone, keeps the interaction productive

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to a blunt comment
Asks a specific, actionable clarifying question rather than guessing
Avoids escalating tone or making it personal
Explains why acting on an unclear comment wastes time

questions.title: You disagree with a requested change in a pull request
questions.prompt: A teammate requests a change on your pull request that you genuinely think would make the code worse, not better. How do you handle the disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't silently comply with a change the author believes is wrong just to avoid friction, and it doesn't dig in and refuse without explanation either -- it explains the specific reasoning behind the current approach and the specific concern with the requested change, in the PR thread where the context is visible to both people and anyone else reviewing later. If the disagreement doesn't resolve through that exchange, the right move is a quick synchronous conversation (a short call or in-person chat) rather than an extended back-and-forth in comments, since tone and nuance are easy to lose in asynchronous text, and if it still doesn't resolve, escalating to a third opinion (another senior engineer, a tech lead) rather than either person unilaterally overriding the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just make the change to avoid a disagreement, because if I actually think it makes the code worse, silently complying doesn't serve either of us -- but I also wouldn't just push back with 'no, I disagree' and leave it there. I'd explain my actual reasoning in the PR thread, specifically why I made the choice I did and specifically what I think the suggested change would cost, so there's a real written record of both positions, not just a flat disagreement. If that exchange doesn't settle it after a round or two, I'd suggest jumping on a quick call rather than going back and forth in comments indefinitely, because tone and nuance get lost in text and a five-minute conversation often resolves what ten comments won't. And if we genuinely can't agree after that, I'd bring in a third person -- another senior engineer or whoever's appropriate -- rather than either of us just overriding the other unilaterally.
commonMistakes: Silently making the change despite disagreeing, just to avoid friction
Refusing the change without clearly explaining the specific technical reasoning
Letting the disagreement drag on indefinitely in asynchronous comments instead of moving to a quick conversation
Unilaterally overriding the other person instead of escalating to a third opinion when truly stuck
keyPoints: Neither silent compliance nor flat refusal is the right response to a genuine technical disagreement
Explaining specific reasoning in the PR thread creates a clear record for both people
Moving to a quick synchronous conversation resolves what extended async back-and-forth often can't
A genuinely unresolved disagreement should be escalated to a third opinion, not unilaterally decided

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids silently complying with a change believed to be wrong
Explains specific technical reasoning rather than a vague objection
Proposes moving to a synchronous conversation if async discussion stalls
Proposes escalating to a third opinion if still unresolved

questions.title: Estimating an uncertain AI feature for your manager
questions.prompt: Your manager asks for an estimate on how long it will take to add tool-calling support to your AI feature. You genuinely don't know -- it depends on how reliably the model follows the tool schema, which you haven't tested yet. How do you communicate that uncertainty?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't make up a confident-sounding number to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, and it also doesn't just say 'I don't know' and leave it there -- it names the specific source of uncertainty (model reliability on this particular tool schema is untested) and proposes a concrete way to reduce it quickly: a short time-boxed spike to actually test tool-calling reliability on a representative sample of cases, after which a much more confident estimate can be given. Framing the estimate as a range or as 'I can tell you more after a day of testing' rather than a single fabricated number is more useful to a manager making planning decisions, because an estimate presented with false confidence that turns out wrong damages trust more than an honest 'I need to spend a day finding out' does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just throw out a number that sounds confident but isn't actually grounded in anything, because if it's wrong later, that costs more trust than being upfront now. I'd tell my manager directly: the real uncertainty here is whether the model reliably calls the right tool with valid arguments on our actual schema, and I haven't tested that yet, so any estimate I give right now is close to a guess. What I'd propose instead is a short, time-boxed spike -- say, a day -- specifically to test tool-calling reliability against a representative set of our real cases, and then I can come back with an estimate I actually trust, plus a sense of whether the schema or prompting needs more work first. That's a more useful answer for someone trying to plan than a specific-sounding number I made up to seem decisive.
commonMistakes: Giving a confident-sounding but fabricated estimate to avoid an uncomfortable conversation
Simply saying 'I don't know' without proposing a way to reduce the uncertainty
Not naming the specific source of uncertainty (untested model reliability on this schema)
Treating honesty about uncertainty as a weakness rather than more useful to planning than false confidence
keyPoints: A fabricated confident estimate damages trust more than honest uncertainty does
The specific source of uncertainty should be named clearly, not left vague
Proposing a short, time-boxed spike to reduce uncertainty is more useful than guessing
A range or conditional estimate is more honest and more useful than a single invented number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids fabricating a confident but ungrounded estimate
Names the specific source of uncertainty clearly
Proposes a concrete way to reduce the uncertainty (e.g. a time-boxed spike)
Frames honest uncertainty as more useful to planning than false confidence

questions.title: A teammate force-pushed over shared branch history
questions.prompt: A teammate force-pushed to a shared branch, overwriting commits you and another person had already pushed. How do you handle the immediate situation, and how do you prevent it from happening again?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer addresses the immediate problem calmly and technically before addressing it as a process issue: check git's reflog (or whoever's local clone still has the lost commits, since a force-push only overwrites the remote, not every local copy) to recover the overwritten work if possible, and communicate promptly and specifically with everyone affected about what happened and what's being recovered, rather than letting people discover broken or missing work on their own. Separately, and without making it about blaming the individual, the real fix is a process change: protecting the shared branch so force-pushes require explicit permission or are disabled entirely (a common GitHub branch-protection setting), which prevents this specific failure mode from recurring regardless of who might make the same mistake next.
questions.professionalAnswer: First, I'd stay calm and treat this as a recoverable technical problem, not a crisis -- a force-push only overwrites the remote branch, so there's a good chance the actual commits still exist somewhere, either in someone's local clone that hasn't been touched since, or recoverable via reflog on the machine that did the force-push. I'd communicate quickly and specifically with everyone affected about what happened and what I'm doing to recover it, rather than letting people just discover broken work on their own and wonder what's going on. Once the immediate recovery is handled, I'd raise this as a process gap, not as 'so-and-so made a mistake' -- the actual fix is turning on branch protection for shared branches so force-pushes require explicit permission or are blocked outright, which means this specific failure mode can't happen again regardless of who's working on the branch next.
commonMistakes: Panicking or assuming the lost work is unrecoverable without checking reflog or other local clones
Not communicating promptly and specifically with everyone affected about what happened
Making the follow-up about blaming the individual rather than fixing the underlying process gap
Not proposing branch protection settings that would prevent this failure mode going forward
keyPoints: A force-push only overwrites the remote; local clones or reflog may still hold the lost commits
Prompt, specific communication with everyone affected is important immediately
The follow-up should focus on a process fix, not blaming the individual
Branch protection against force-pushes on shared branches is the concrete preventive fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies recovery options (reflog, other local clones)
Describes prompt, specific communication with affected teammates
Frames the follow-up as a process fix, not blame
Proposes branch protection as the concrete prevention

questions.title: Asked to Grant Urgent SSH Access That Bypasses Normal Key Policy
questions.prompt: A project manager asks you to urgently grant a contractor SSH access to a production server today, and the fastest path would mean skipping your team's usual key-rotation and access-review process 'just this once.' How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't flatly refuse the urgency, and it doesn't quietly skip the process either -- it separates the two problems: the actual urgency (contractor needs access today) and the process shortcut being proposed (skipping review), and solves the first without accepting the second. In practice that means granting access through the normal mechanism but expedited -- generating a properly scoped key pair for the contractor specifically, with access limited to only what they actually need, and getting whoever normally approves access to sign off quickly rather than skip the approval entirely -- so the urgency is met without creating an unreviewed, undocumented access grant that nobody will remember to clean up later. If the normal process genuinely can't move fast enough today, the honest move is naming that specifically to the project manager and proposing the fastest compliant alternative, rather than being the one who quietly broke the policy under pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just quietly skip the review to avoid an awkward conversation, and I also wouldn't flatly say no to a genuinely urgent business need -- I'd separate the two things being asked for. The urgency is real and solvable; the shortcut being proposed is the part I'd push back on. So I'd generate a key pair scoped specifically to what this contractor actually needs -- not broad standing access -- and go get whoever normally signs off on access to approve it quickly, rather than skipping that approval entirely. If the normal process genuinely can't move fast enough today, I'd say that directly to the project manager rather than quietly deciding to bypass it myself, because an untracked, unreviewed access grant is exactly the kind of thing that turns into a real incident six months later when nobody remembers it exists. I'd rather be the person who found the fastest compliant path than the one who quietly broke policy under pressure.
commonMistakes: Quietly skipping the access-review process to avoid an awkward conversation with the project manager
Flatly refusing the request without proposing a faster compliant alternative
Granting overly broad access instead of scoping it specifically to what the contractor needs
Not documenting or communicating the grant, leaving an untracked access credential nobody remembers later
keyPoints: Separates the genuine urgency from the proposed process shortcut, and solves the first without accepting the second
Proposes an expedited but still-reviewed path rather than skipping approval entirely
Scopes the contractor's access specifically to what's actually needed, not broad standing access
Communicates honestly if the normal process genuinely can't move fast enough, rather than quietly bypassing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates urgency from the process shortcut
Proposes an expedited but still-compliant path
Emphasizes scoping access appropriately
Shows honest communication rather than silent bypass

questions.title: Your Team Keeps Rerunning a Flaky Pipeline Instead of Fixing It
questions.prompt: Your CI pipeline's test stage fails intermittently, and you've noticed your teammates have gotten into the habit of just clicking 'rerun' until it passes instead of investigating. How do you address this as a team practice issue?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just quietly keep rerunning it too, and it also doesn't unilaterally decide to fix it alone without raising the pattern with the team -- a flaky test that gets rerun into passing is actively dangerous because it erodes the entire point of automated testing: if 'rerun until green' becomes normal, a genuinely new, real failure can get waved through the same way, and nobody will notice until it's a production incident. The right move is naming the pattern explicitly to the team (not blaming any individual, since the habit likely formed gradually and reasonably under deadline pressure), proposing concrete next steps -- identifying specifically which test(s) are flaky, treating flakiness itself as a bug worth a ticket and some investigation time rather than an annoyance to route around, and in the meantime making flaky reruns visible (e.g. tracking how often a given test needs a rerun) rather than invisible, so the team can see the actual scope of the problem instead of each person normalizing it individually.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just join in and start rerunning it too, because a flaky test that gets rerun into passing isn't a minor annoyance -- it quietly erodes the entire point of automated testing. If 'click rerun until it's green' becomes the normal move, a genuinely new, real failure can slip through disguised as 'just more flakiness,' and nobody notices until it's an actual production incident. I'd raise the pattern with the team directly, without making it about any one person, since this kind of habit usually forms gradually and reasonably under deadline pressure, not out of carelessness. Then I'd propose something concrete: let's actually name which specific test or tests are flaky, treat that flakiness as a real bug worth a ticket and some investigation time instead of something to route around, and in the meantime, let's make the rerun pattern visible -- tracking how often a given test needs a rerun -- rather than something each of us is quietly normalizing on our own. I'd also offer to take the first pass at investigating it myself, since raising the problem without offering to help fix it isn't much better than not raising it at all.
commonMistakes: Joining the habit of rerunning without flagging it as a real problem
Blaming individual teammates for a habit that formed gradually under normal pressure
Not proposing a concrete next step, just naming the problem without a path forward
Letting flaky-test reruns stay invisible instead of actually tracking how often it happens
keyPoints: Routinely rerunning a flaky test until green erodes the real value of automated testing
The pattern should be raised with the team directly, without blaming any individual
Flakiness itself should be treated as a bug worth investigating, not routed around
Making rerun frequency visible helps the team see the actual scope of the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real risk of normalized flaky reruns
Raises the issue constructively with the team, not as individual blame
Proposes treating flakiness as a trackable bug to investigate
Proposes making the pattern visible rather than letting it stay hidden
